packs.title: Memorials, Museums and Civic Life
packs.promise: Explore Washington through major memorials, Smithsonian museums and civic landmarks.

q.s: Notice how different objects solve different problems.
st: Choose open galleries included with your pass.
Find a shape related to lift, a feature for protection and a way of communicating information.
Use a label to explain one design choice.

q.s: Look for different ways scientists learn about the world.
st: Choose open exhibits and leave circulation clear.
Find a specimen, a model and an explanation of a research method.
Record how a label distinguishes evidence from reconstruction.

q.s: Learn about a civic building through the people and objects associated with it.
st: Use an open visitor-center exhibit.
Choose a factual detail about the building’s work or daily operations.
Record the source and one question it raises.

packs.title: Small Wonders, Grand City
packs.promise: Find the intimate details inside a monumental day.

q.s: Collect three ways a plant can draw an edge.
st: Enter the open outdoor gardens beside the Conservatory and choose a public path with plants visible at a comfortable height.
Find three different leaf or stem outlines: one smooth, one divided or toothed, and one long or narrow. Branches and dry seed heads can replace leaves out of season.
Record each outline with a few words or a permitted photo. Read a plant label if you want a name; do not guess a species or what is edible.
Choose one outline and describe an everyday object it reminds you of, keeping your comparison separate from a botanical fact.

q.s: Turn a grand view into one small composition.
st: Choose an open public-sidewalk view near the Conservatory that includes the Capitol dome or another clear portion of the Capitol exterior.
Find a small foreground detail already in place, such as a leaf, fence curve, or pavement joint. Do not move or hold anything against the building.
Compose the small detail and the distant architecture together, in a photo or a written description. Give the small detail as much attention as the landmark.
Write a two-sentence postcard: first the small detail, then the grand view it changed for you.

q.s: Make the trip between places part of the memory.
st: Begin at the marked crossing near Fourteenth Street and Madison Drive NW. Once across, choose an open public path toward the Washington Monument.
Walk or roll only a comfortable distance. Before moving, choose a distant landmark or roofline; compare its position with one nearby tree or path edge at two stopping places.
Notice how much attention shifts when a landmark becomes part of the route rather than the destination.
Save your two viewpoint notes and one thing the in-between space added to your day.
